---
title: "The model"
---

The model is an agent-based stress test of 67 euro-area significant institutions.
A shock weakens banks' capital and triggers depositor runs; each bank then meets its
liquidity need by choosing among four funding channels — outright **sales**,
**unsecured** borrowing, private **repo**, and **central-bank credit** — and those
choices feed back into asset prices and into each other through a multi-week cascade.

The visual below shows the mechanism the paper is about: **how banks move through the
capital–liquidity plane as the cascade unfolds, and how the collateral framework
changes that path.**

## Banks in the capital–liquidity plane

Each point is a **group of banks** (by home country; countries with fewer than three
banks are pooled into "Other euro area", so nothing here identifies an individual
institution). The horizontal axis is the CET1 capital ratio, the vertical axis the
liquidity coverage ratio. Move the **intensity** slider to choose how severe the
shock is, and the **step** slider to walk the cascade forward week by week. The left
panel is the sales-only world; the right panel adds the full framework.

Watch what happens as you advance the steps: under **sales only** the groups drift
down and to the left — fire sales erode both capital and liquidity — while under the
**full framework** they hold much closer to where they started, because pledging
raises liquidity without forcing capital-eroding sales.

```{ojs}
raw = FileAttachment("../data/phase_space.csv").csv({typed: true})
```

```{ojs}
viewof intensity = Inputs.range([0.1, 1.0], {step: 0.1, value: 0.5, label: "Shock intensity"})
viewof step = Inputs.range([0, 14], {step: 1, value: 14, label: "Cascade step (week)"})
```

```{ojs}
armLabel = ({S: "Sales only", SURC: "Full framework"})
shown = raw.filter(d => Math.abs(d.intensity - intensity) < 1e-9 && d.step <= step)
now = shown.filter(d => d.step === step)
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 900,
  height: 420,
  grid: true,
  fx: {
    domain: ["S", "SURC"],
    label: null,
    tickFormat: a => armLabel[a]
  },
  x: {label: "CET1 ratio (%)"},
  y: {label: "LCR (%)"},
  color: {legend: true, label: "Country group"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(shown, {
      x: "cet1_pct", y: "lcr_pct",
      z: d => d.group + d.arm, fx: "arm",
      stroke: "group", strokeOpacity: 0.35, strokeWidth: 1
    }),
    Plot.dot(now, {
      x: "cet1_pct", y: "lcr_pct", fx: "arm",
      fill: "group", r: 6, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 0.6,
      tip: true,
      title: d => `${d.group}: CET1 ${d.cet1_pct.toFixed(1)}%, LCR ${d.lcr_pct.toFixed(1)}% (${d.n_banks} banks)`
    })
  ]
})
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How to read this
Trajectories are cross-seed averages over ten simulation seeds, aggregated to
country groups of at least three banks. The two panels share axes, so a group's
horizontal position is directly comparable across the sales-only and full-framework
worlds. Source: group-aggregated headline results; see the data provenance note in
the repository.
:::

## Collateral-conditional liquidity

The heart of the model is a simple idea: **the same asset is worth a different amount
of liquidity depending on how you try to raise cash against it.** A bank can *sell* an
asset (and take a price discount), *repo* it (and take a private haircut), or *pledge*
it at the *central bank* (and take the Eurosystem haircut). An asset that is nearly
cash-good in one channel can be useless in another.

### Why the channels differ

Pick an asset below. The bars show, illustratively, how much usable liquidity €1 of
that asset yields in each channel — and the note explains why.

```{ojs}
archetypes = [
  {asset: "Government bond", sales: 0.90, repo: 0.98, cb: 0.99,
   why: "Deep market and a tiny haircut: liquid in every channel, and best of all at the central bank."},
  {asset: "Covered bond", sales: 0.85, repo: 0.94, cb: 0.93,
   why: "Marketable and eligible: sellable at a modest discount, and pledgeable in both repo and at the central bank."},
  {asset: "Corporate bond", sales: 0.72, repo: 0.80, cb: 0.85,
   why: "Thinner market and larger haircuts, but still usable in all three channels."},
  {asset: "Bank loan (credit claim)", sales: 0.00, repo: 0.00, cb: 0.65,
   why: "Non-marketable: it cannot be sold or repo'd at all. Only the central bank accepts it — at a haircut — which is exactly what the collateral framework controls."},
  {asset: "Equity", sales: 0.60, repo: 0.00, cb: 0.00,
   why: "Sellable at a discount, but ineligible as collateral anywhere: no repo, no central-bank credit."}
]
viewof pick = Inputs.select(archetypes, {label: "Asset", format: d => d.asset})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 220, width: 640, marginLeft: 120,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Usable liquidity per €1", tickFormat: "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: false},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX([
      {channel: "Sell", v: pick.sales},
      {channel: "Repo", v: pick.repo},
      {channel: "Central bank", v: pick.cb}
    ], {y: "channel", x: "v", fill: "channel", sort: {y: null}}),
    Plot.text([
      {channel: "Sell", v: pick.sales},
      {channel: "Repo", v: pick.repo},
      {channel: "Central bank", v: pick.cb}
    ], {y: "channel", x: "v", text: d => d.v === 0 ? "unusable" : (d.v * 100).toFixed(0) + "¢",
        dx: 6, textAnchor: "start"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
md`**${pick.asset}.** ${pick.why}`
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
These five archetypes use rounded, illustrative haircuts to convey the mechanism; the
next chart shows the actual schedule.
:::

### The realised schedule

Averaged over the actual Eurosystem eligibility and haircut schedule (and the LCH repo
schedule and the sales-discount calibration), here is the liquidity value of €1 in each
channel by asset category. The pattern the model turns on is stark: **loans and credit
claims are essentially unusable except at the central bank**, while government paper is
usable everywhere.

```{ojs}
chl = FileAttachment("../data/channel_liquidity.csv").csv({typed: true})
chLabel = ({sales: "Sell", repo: "Repo", cb: "Central bank"})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 900, height: 380, marginLeft: 160,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Usable liquidity per €1", tickFormat: "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  fy: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["sales", "repo", "cb"],
          tickFormat: c => chLabel[c], label: "Channel"},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(chl, {
      x: "liquidity_value", y: "channel", fill: "channel", fy: "category",
      sort: {y: null}
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```
